Messages.Author: David Cherryholmes
Messages.Body:
Clandestine Contract [FN:C2]
Cardtype: Action

Clan: Assamite

Cost: 1 pool

Contract.
Requires an Assamite with a capacity above 4. +1 stealth action.
(D) Enter combat with a ready minion controlled by another Methuselah and
put this card on that minion. This Assamite is chosen for this
contract. This Assamite may enter combat with the minion with this card as
a +1 stealth (D) action.

Can an Assamite play this card to enter combat with a minion, then Freak
Drive and re-enter combat with the same minion? Obviously it's from the
same card, so I'd think not, but the redundant language on the card got me
wondering if the two rushes are considered to be from seperate sources.

Messages.Author: Colin McGuigan
Messages.Body:
David Cherryholmes wrote:
> Can an Assamite play this card to enter combat with a minion, then Freak
> Drive and re-enter combat with the same minion?

No, because it's still the same card (the redundant language just states
that you can continue to rush in future turns). If the Assamite had two
Clandestine Contracts on the minion (played on two different turns),
then they could rush twice, though.

--Colin McGuigan

What it *does* allow, however, is a combination with Fame. If you're
trying one of the repetitive Fame/rescue decks, two cards let you get in
another rush. Without CC, you'd either have to use a Rush, an untap, a
Rush. or you'd have to use up a potentially expensive master phase and

Messages.Body:
In message <4920...@web2news.com>, robtreasure <robtreasure.news.inval

>> A card slot saved is a card slot you can spend on making
>> Fame/Rescue/Repeat work less badly.
>
>Innnnnnteresting. Am I correct in thinking that you think of this a duff
>combo / tactic? I think it's pretty darn workable myself.

I think it's workable but...

Unlike most combat-oriented decks, it works based on the fact that
you're going to give them the vampire back. Yes, careful planning can
mean that you can try to organise so that Parnassus rushes, Harika
rescues and then Parnassus rushes again *but* in between time, the
target deck may have cycled some cards (there's quite a few actions in
there it could react to - intercept, Wake (Forced, in this instance))
and you could find yourself on the wrong end of Skin of Rock and
suddenly that guaranteed torpor is suddenly an active vampire.

Assamite combat - Taste of Death isn't the only card in the world, first
round aggravated damage is moderately tricky to garner properly.
Weapons or something. So death by massive damage (or blood loss, which
is the same for this purpose) is quite possible and, if you're going for
anti-Fortitude, moderately likely - Blood Sweat, Exuding Blood, and so
on, with gun support? So lots of people going to torpor are doing it
via blood loss and hitting zero. So when you rescue, you'll end up
spending some blood. Probably not on EVERY minion, but on some, at
least. So combat - which is blood intensive and scary - is being hurt
by losing some blood too.

Unlike most of the obvious successful strategies, for Fame/Torpor/Repeat
to work, you need Fame. This makes it very, very master intensive and
susceptible. Which also screws up your play of Sudden Reversal and
Direct Intervention, losing the flexibility for which is a pain.
Obviously, any deck using masters has those issues - but they seem to be
less expensive, opportunity wise. Everyone wants to play Blood Doll,
everyone wants to play Minion Tap but you don't have to spend a turn
thinking "I can't do my deck if I don't play it this turn" in usual
circumstances. (Obviously, in the late game with little pool and so on
it's different.)

So you don't have innate untap to make it more efficient, so need to
play some of the trickier vampires, are losing blood (if not
haemorrhaging it under bad conditions) and can't keep the vampires down
properly...

It's certainly playable, and it's certainly something you can do well
with. But combat decks that rely on curtailing their offence seem
tricky.

>When are we going to see you again anyway? Tourneys aren't the same
>without you dude.

With luck, I should be able to play at this month's Watford tournament.
I'm in Cambridge for the fortnight before, so how I'll get down to the
tournament, and where I'll be the night before, is anyone's guess.

On Tue, 8 Jul 2003, robtreasure wrote:

> Both of Clandestine's rushes are +1 Stealth which is great for hitting
> the target and being able to deliver the goods more times than not,
> which if you ask me is what successful rush decks are all about.

I think the big design hurdle for the Assamites is answering the question
"what do I do after I torpor them?" Burn, Graverob, diablerize with Tariq
or disposable minions.... these are some possible answers, of
course. Generating enough minion actions to be effective at rushing used
to seem like the insurmountable obstacle, but the deck we're talking
around has that covered.

<snip guns are good>

> Agreed. I do however think some support is almost essential in the form
> of Prevention for when you get nasty stuff like DotB played on you or
> maybe Terror Frenzy to counter _all_ other close range.

Definitely. It's just that, considered over a large number of combats,
you generally won't *need* to have that stuff to be the winner.

> That one cost on Freak does add up if
> you are using it in any heavy quantity though.

Were you playing with many Tastes? It's a card with diminishing returns,
but even if your target has only has one blood, it'll break you even for
the next rush. With decks like Laz or Fatima + AR, the default damage is
so high that scooping blood from a Taste every two or three combats will
keep you going.

> Nice, I think it's a powerful archetype. Very open to one vamp sew up
> tactics (Sensory Dep, PTO etc.) but still very nasty.

Yup. I think Secure Haven is important for this deck, beyond simply
contesting it away from targets, but you'll always have that one vamp
vulnerability. Blitzkrieging whoever may pose that threat may be
required. Certainly in that six-way last night I had already worked
out who needed to get victory points in what order for me to win. It's
also good to understand how to affect your grand-predator or grand-prey by
pushing or pulling on your predator or prey. That tends to nudge the
table in the right direction without blatantly rushing
cross-table. People playing one vampire decks need to think about these
things more than others.

Messages.Author: David Cherryholmes
Messages.Body:
On 11 Jul 2003, Ben Peal wrote:

> The irony being that it is _you_ who are intimidated by your predator,
> causing you to implement the rush-defense strategy.

We could easily get distracted by the semantics of "intimidation". I'm
always intimidated by my predator in one sense, since he's trying to oust
me and I assume he's got a good deck. What I meant by my comment was
that, if you have a clearly demonstrated ability to back oust, *some*
players can be convinced to slow down their attacks. Against some other
players, it is possible to trim back their minions to something you can
survive, without them throwing a hissy fit and influencing themselves
out. Only some, though. The others I guess you go ahead and erase, for
lack of any better options.

> I'm not really a fan of "just barely", so I'd be inclined to throw some
> extra bleed in there to hasten the process. (and presumably you're
> using Fame and/or Tension)

I'm an enormous fan of "just barely". I would like to get the job done
with exactly the amount of resources required and not a bit more (there
are parallels here with the 80 card deck philosophy). The
counterbalancing notion is my equal belief in the need for "slop". So I
tend to build decks that aim for just barely, and just a smidgeon
more. For example, I'd say a primary payload of Fame-dunk, with followup
bleeds for one or two a turn, is just barely + a smidgeon.

> :) I've been addicted to Wakes for basically the same reason.

I've just got no deck-building discipline for Wakes. Maybe we can chew on
that over GenCon. I mean, yeah, I've got decks with Wakes, a few with
lots, but I don't see how these other people I play with (who are pretty
good), always manage to squeeze in a block of them in any deck they
play. I'm probably overcompensating somewhere that I can't see.

> You've got a longer-term ousting strategy, and as the game wears on
> and you're only getting one or two from the Tastes, you'll be looking
> at the Hunting Grounds differently.

I toyes last night with putting a HG in. It's more to do with the pool
cost and the Mastercard slot than with not thinking the effects are good.

> *shrug* I'd still like to have that backup vamp with CEL.

I just don't see the wisdom in putting 5 pool worth of gun in the hands of
someone who could very well get punked. It may even be handing out that
gun to an opponent. Still, that's a very specific deck. Generally I
agree with you.

It's all a matter of degree. A rush-combat deck isn't going to be
ousting its prey solely by Fame or Tension in the Ranks. It's going
to throw some bleeds in there. A bruise-bleed deck is likely going
to have Fame or Tension to supplement the bleeds and discourage
blocking.

Unless I'm playing weenie-rush, I consider bleeds for one to be a
bad plan for a rush-combat deck. Hence the desire for some extra
bleed cards.

Xian <xi...@visi.nospam.com> writes:

> > I see Wakes as being similar to Freak Drives in that they help you
> > generate additional actions that would have otherwise been simply
> > vampires left untapped to defend.
>
> Given the choice, do you prefer Wake or Freak? Freak costs, but maybe
> allows more options? Less surprise, though.

Well, it's one of those "It depends" questions. Daddy or chips?

However, surprise isn't an altogether good thing, necessarily so.
Consider the player who, on seeing you untapped, decides not to
attempt the bleed in the first place and so keeps their hand more
clogged. Which may or may not be better than the player who attempts
it, cycling cards, and sees you play Wake. That will, of course,
depend on all sorts of factors. A toolboxy deck will suffer somewhat
if the cards are played, but then you Wake, because it may not be able
to amass that bleed offence easily again, whereas a one trick pony
deck will just keep on pulling.
